## The Log Source

Listing 7-4 shows an example of a log source.

Listing 7-4: syslog-ng Configuration for iptables — Source

```
source src {
# include internal syslog-ng messages
# note: the internal() source is required!
#
internal();
#
# the following line will be replaced by the
# socket list generated by SuConfig using
# variables from /etc/sysconfig/syslog:
#unix-dgram("/dev/log/")
unix-dgram("/var/lib/ntp/dev/log/")

#
# uncomment to process log messages from network:
#udp("0.0.0.0") port(514);
}
```

Listing 7-4 shows suggested definition for the syslog-ng process. This example shows two sources, /dev/log (for the standard kernel logging device) and /var/lib/ntp/dev/log. A separate entry is necessary because the NTP service runs in a jail its log source has to reside under that jail so that the npc can access it.

This example also shows a UDP entry that SUSE has commented out. This is a logging source for a network port. This is how you can set up a central logging server for your organization. By setting a source to UDP on port 514, you are enabling your machine to accept messages for logging from remote hosts. TCP/IP port 514 on UDP is the standard port for syslog messages. If you uncomment this entry, you are able to receive messages from remote hosts.

For more information on TCP/IP and specifying addresses and ports in Linux, see Chapters 6 and 15.

## The Filter

Listing 7-5 gives an example of a syslog-ng filter.

| Listing 7-5: The Filter |
| f_iptables { facility(kernel) and match("IN") and match("OUT"); }; |

A filter in syslog-ng is the same as the first field in the syslog.conf file but has the capability to be much more granular. In the example shown in Listing 7-5, you are defining a filter named f iptables. This filter filters out messages that have the log-facility of kernel and uses a regular expression to match a message if it contains the words IN or OUT. The regular expression capabilities of syslog-ng enable to eliminate or redirect logging messages based on their contents.

> We talk about iptables in detail in Chapter 24. Now, you can use iptables to log messages about TCP/IP packet with a message prefix. For example, you can say that a message has been denied Into your machine/network, then the message is prefixed with the word IN. It is true for any messages that have been denied OUT of your network. In this case, you could tell syslog-ng to log these facts into a separate file for your perusal at a convenient time.

## The Log Destination

Listing 7-6 shows an example of a log destination.

| Listing 7-6: The Destination |
| destination firewall { file("/var/log/firewall"); }; |

By default, SUSE comments this line out in order to send these messages to its default location. With most services in SUSE, all output is sent to the /var/log/messages file because there is not a logging facility for each specific service. So we assume we have uncommented the destination for use on our system that firewall goes to a specific destination. The destination specifies that the custom definition firewall will write log messages to the file /var/log/firewall. This enables you to examine firewall-related messages (produced by the iptables facility, which filters network packets) by simply examining a specific log file.

## The Log Definition – Tying It All Together

These three definitions may sound well and good in principle, but are you getting the feeling that there should be something to bring these three definitions together? This is the final piece in the puzzle of syslog-ng. You need to configure a log parameter that will use these definitions and bring them into a coherent for a logging trigger, which is a log definition that ties a log source, filter, and destination together.

Listing 7-7 brings together their disparate example definitions of log source, filter, and log destination into a final log definition.

### 7-7: Log Definition

```
log { source(src); filter(iptables); destination(firewall); };
```

For any log entry you want to make, you need to specify the logging source (in this case /dev/log and /var/lib/ntp/dev/log), the filter (anything from the kernel that contains either IN= or OUT=), and the destination (in the case file /var/log/firewall).

You should now have enough information to help you set up syslog-ng and distinguish why and where you use syslog-ng and its more granular control compared to what syslog offers. As you can see, you can ultimately do powerful things with syslog-ng by combining network sources with complicated filters.

## Future Directions for Linux Logging

Although this chapter discussed two different system logging applications for Linux, there are actually many more, each designed to solve or simplify types of logging concerns.

One of the more interesting developments in system logging is the evlog (Event Log) application originally developed by IBM for use in its enterprise AIX environments and later released to the open source community. Although still maturing, evlog project is an ambitious effort that is POSIX-compliant and platform-independent, and can significantly simplify logging in a complex multi-machine environment.
